name: Three-quarters of an inch standing in for five
symptom: A frame house whose window and door openings are trimmed with a flat board 3 1/2 to 5 1/2 in wide and 3/4 in thick, square-edged, with no backband, no moulded edge and no cap. The opening reads as a line drawn round the glass. In the worst version the trim is 1/2 in urethane or a J-channel with nothing in it at all.

cause.explanation: A frame wall gives its window a reveal of 3/4 to 2 in and no more — that is all a 2x6 wall with sheathing has. The period answer was to buy the depth back with a 5-6 in architrave built up of two or three members: a flat casing, a backband standing 3/4 to 1 in proud of it, and often a moulded cap. The modern answer is one piece of 1x4 or 1x6 in whatever the trim package is, because a backband is a second SKU, a second cut list and a second nailing operation, and because the window manufacturer's flange detail wants a single flat plane to lap onto.
cause.cost_saved: A three-member architrave with a backband runs $9-$18 per lineal foot installed against $3.50-$6 for flat stock. On thirty openings, $2,400-$5,000.

rule_violated.statement: 3/4 to 2 in of reveal plus a 5-6 in architrave doing the work the depth cannot. The opposite assembly reaching the same effect.

rule_violated.ref: trim-classical / casing.width = opening_width / 6 = 6 in at a 3 ft opening; casing.projection = opening_width / 6 * 0.18 = 1 1/16 in
rule_violated.statement: The casing's projection is 18 per cent of its width. Six inches wide and one inch proud is the target; six inches wide and three-quarters of an inch proud is 30 per cent short and reads it.
The window surround runs slightly wider than the door casing on the same wall.

rule_violated.ref: a frame wall has no depth, so all of its depth is in its trim
rule_violated.statement: Masonry and frame reach the same effect by opposite assemblies. Removing the architrave from a frame wall is exactly equivalent to removing the reveal from a masonry one.

correct_practice: Build the architrave in members. A Georgian or Colonial Revival window surround on a frame wall is 5 to 6 1/2 in wide overall and stands 1 to 1 3/8 in proud of the cladding at its outer edge, made as a flat casing 4-5 in wide with a backband of 1 1/4-1 3/4 in projecting 3/4-1 in beyond it, and it carries a moulded cap or a shallow cornice at the head with a wash and a drip. The rule of thumb from the trim pack is a width of one sixth of the opening and a projection of 18 per cent of that width — at a 3 ft opening, 6 in wide and 1 1/16 in proud. Below about 3/4 in of total projection the surround stops throwing a shadow at any sun angle and the opening reverts to a hole.

fixes.right: Casing plus backband plus a moulded head cap with a drip, all in one wood or a cellular PVC that will hold an arris; 6 in wide, 1 1/8 in proud minimum, mitred or butted with the head running past the jambs.
fixes.cheap: Add a backband to the flat stock you already have. A single ripped 1x2 with a bevelled or ogee outer edge, nailed to the outer edge of the existing casing, costs about $1.20 a lineal foot and turns a 3/4 in flat board into a 1 3/4 in stepped architrave. This one move recovers most of the shadow for roughly $250 a house, and it is the highest-return dollar in the whole envelope group. If even that is refused, widen the flat casing from 3 1/2 to 5 1/2 in — width is free and partially substitutes for depth, because a wide flat band at least reads as a member.
fixes.dishonest: Urethane or polystyrene 'architrave' with a moulded profile at 1/2 to 5/8 in of relief. It has the right shape at 4 ft and none of the right depth at 40, because the moulding's members are each about 1/8 in and every one of them falls below the threshold at which a profile casts a legible shadow. Also dishonest: painting the casing a strong contrasting colour to make it read — which substitutes a graphic outline for relief, and is precisely what a classical profile is not doing.

detection: Measure the shadow, not the width. In an image with directional light, the casing should throw a dark band along its shaded edge roughly equal to its projection: 1 in of projection at a 45 degree sun is a 1 in shadow, easily 1/4 of the casing's own width. If the casing edge is a hairline with no tonal step, the projection is under 1/4 in and the fault is present regardless of what the casing width is. Second, look for the backband step: a correct architrave shows TWO parallel lines along its outer edge, the casing face and the backband face, at different tones. One line means one member. Third, at the head: a correct surround has a cap that projects past the jambs on both sides by 1-2 in with returned ends. A head casing flush with the jamb casings, mitred at the corners like a picture frame, is the flat-stock tell.

exceptions.why: Window trim 2 to 3 in wide or absent is definitional, and openings are meant to look punched rather than framed. A full architrave would contradict the continuous skin.
exceptions.bounds: The trim must be genuinely narrow AND the shingles must run tight to it — the effect depends on the skin's continuity, not on a thin picture frame. A 3 1/2 in flat casing with a J-channel round it is not this exception.

bounds_test.note: Genuinely narrow AND the shingles run tight to it. A 3 1/2 in flat casing with a J-channel round it fails both halves and is not this exception.

applies_when.note: Holds only where the skin is shingle and continuous over the opening's surroundings.

exceptions.why: Broad, flat, unmoulded trim is the style's stated method: ornament by profile and mass rather than by relief carving. Greek Revival casings are wide and deliberately plain.
exceptions.bounds: Wide means wide — 6 to 10 in — and flat means unmoulded, not thin. The Greek Revival casing is the BROADEST of the three families in the trim pack, and it stands proud of the wall with a crisp square arris. Flatness of profile with full width and a real 1 in step is the exception; a narrow thin board is not.

bounds_test.note: Wide means 6-10 in and flat means unmoulded, not thin. The Greek Revival casing is the broadest of the three families in the trim pack and still stands 1 in proud with a crisp square arris.

applies_when.note: Flat profile at full width and full step — a moulding change, not a dimension change.

exceptions.why: Craftsman trim is flat and unmoulded with a projecting head cap and often no backband, and its expression is in the head, the sill and the wide flat jamb boards.
exceptions.bounds: The head cap must project 1 1/2-2 1/2 in with a wash and a drip; Craftsman moves the depth from the jamb to the head rather than deleting it.

bounds_test.note: Craftsman moves the depth from the jamb to the head. The head cap must project 1 1/2-2 1/2 in with a wash and a drip; a flat head casing flush with the jambs is the fault.

exceptions.why: No applied trim anywhere; the opening is deeply recessed in a thick rendered wall and the depth comes from the reveal.
exceptions.bounds: Requires a genuine reveal of 8 in or more with a rounded arris. Two inches of stucco over frame with a flush window is the revival failing at its own test — the style node itself names reveal depth as the tell against the genuine article.

bounds_test.note: Two inches of stucco over frame with a flush window is the revival failing at its own test.

exceptions.why: Same reasoning: mass wall, deep reveal, no architrave, and a limewashed or painted band round the opening instead.
exceptions.bounds: Wall must be genuinely 500-700 mm; the painted surround is a colour gesture on top of real depth, not a substitute for it.

bounds_test.note: 500 mm. The painted surround is a colour gesture on top of real depth, not a substitute for it.

confused_with.difference: The masonry twin of this fault. Diagnose the wall first: a masonry wall needs the reveal and takes NO architrave; a frame wall has no reveal and needs the architrave. Applying either cure to the other wall produces a new fault.

sources: Asher Benjamin, The American Builder's Companion (1806), plates of window and door architraves
NPS Preservation Brief 16: Substitute Materials on Historic Building Exteriors

test.note: The trim pack's own figure: casing.projection = opening_width / 6 * 0.18, so a 6 in casing stands 1 1/16 in proud. Measure the shadow, not the width — at a 45 degree sun the shaded edge of the casing throws a dark band equal to its projection, roughly a quarter of the casing's own width. A hairline edge with no tonal step means the ratio is under about 0.05 and the fault is present regardless of how wide the casing is.

secondary_tests.note: One sixth of the opening: 6 in at a 3 ft window. Width partially substitutes for depth because a wide flat band at least reads as a member, which is why widening stock casing from 3 1/2 to 5 1/2 in is a real if partial fix.
The absolute floor. Below 3/4 in of total projection the surround stops throwing a shadow at any sun angle and the opening reverts to a hole.

A correct architrave shows TWO parallel lines along its outer edge at different tones — the casing face and the backband face. One line means one member, and one member means the depth is whatever the stock thickness was.

severity_by_style.why: Trim of 2-3 in or none is definitional; there is no architrave to fail.
No applied trim anywhere on the exterior.
Ornament by profile and mass rather than by relief carving means the broad flat casing is carrying the entire expressive load; thin it and there is nothing left.

inverted_by.statement: An applied architrave is the fault. Depth comes from a reveal of 8 in or more with a rounded arris, and the style node names reveal depth as the tell against the genuine article.
As above: mass wall, deep reveal, no architrave, and a limewashed painted band round the opening instead.
A full architrave is the fault, because it frames an opening the style wants to read as punched through a continuous skin.
